疏奏不納。 歲餘，安樂公主被誅。
The memorial was not accepted. A little over a year later, Princess Anle was executed.
19
睿宗即位，又為金仙、玉真公主廣營二觀。 先是，中宗時斜封受官人一切停任，凡數百千人，又有敕放令卻上。 替否時為左補闕，又上疏陳時政曰：臣嘗以為古之用度不時，爵賞不當，破家亡國者，口說不如身逢，耳聞不如眼見，臣請以有唐已來理國之得失，陛下之所眼見者以言之。 惟陛下審之聽之，擇善而從之，則萬歲之業，自可致矣，何憂乎黎庶之不康，福祚之不永！ 伏以太宗文武聖皇帝，陛下之祖，撥亂反正，開階立極，得至理之體，設簡要之方。 省其官，清其吏，舉天下職司無一虛授，用天下財帛無一枉費。 賞必俟功，官必得俊，所為無不成，所征無不伏。 不多造寺觀而福德自至，不多度僧尼而殃咎自滅。 道合乎天地，德通乎神明。 故天地憐之，神明祐之，使陰陽不愆，風雨合度。 四人樂其業，五谷遂其成，腐粟爛帛，填街委巷。 千里萬里，貢賦於郊； 九夷百蠻，歸款於闕。 自有帝皇已來，未有若斯之神聖者也，故得享國久長，多歷年所，陛下何不取而則之？ 中宗孝和皇帝，陛下之兄，居先人之業，忽先人之化，不取賢良之言，而恣子女之意。 官爵非擇，虛食祿者數千人； 封建無功，妄食土者百餘戶。 造寺不止，枉費財者數百億； 度人不休，免租庸者數十萬。 是使國家所出加數倍，所入減數倍。 倉不停卒歲之儲，庫不貯一時之帛。 所惡者逐，逐多忠良； 所愛者賞，賞多讒慝。 朋佞喋喋，交相傾動。 容身不為於朝廷，保位皆由於黨附。 奪百姓之食，以養殘兇； 剝萬人之衣，以塗土木。 於是人怨神怒，親忿眾離，水旱不調，疾疫屢起。 遠近殊論，公私罄然。 五六年間，再三禍變，享國不永，受終於兇婦人。 寺舍不能保其身，僧尼不能護妻子，取譏萬代，見笑四夷。 此陛下之所眼見也，何不除而改之。 依太宗之理國，則百官以理，百姓無憂，故太山之安立可致矣； 依中宗之理國，則萬人以怨，百事不寧，故累卵之危立可致矣。 頃自夏已來，霪雨不解，谷荒於壟，麥爛於場。 入秋已來，亢旱成災，苗而不實，霜損蟲暴，草葉枯黃。 下人咨嗟，未知赒賑； 而營寺造觀，日繼於時，檢校試官，充臺溢署。 伏惟陛下愛兩女，為造兩觀，燒瓦運木，載土填坑，道路流言，皆云計用錢百餘萬貫。 惟陛下，聖人也，無所不知； 陛下，明君也，無所不見。 既知且見，知倉有幾年之儲，庫有幾年之帛？ 知百姓之間可存活乎？ 三邊之上可轉輸乎？ 當今發一卒以禦邊陲，遣一兵以衛社稷，多無衣食，皆帶饑寒。 賞賜之間，迥無所出，軍旅驟敗，莫不由斯。 而乃以百萬貫錢造無用之觀，以受六合之怨乎！ 以違萬人之心乎！ 伏惟陛下續阿韋之醜跡，而不改阿韋之亂政。 忍棄太宗之理本，不忍棄中宗之亂階； 忍棄太宗久長之謀，不忍棄中宗短促之計。 陛下又何以繼祖宗、觀萬國。 昔陛下為皇太子，在阿韋之時，危亡是懼，常切齒於群兇。 今貴為天子，富有海內，而不改群兇之事，臣恐復有切齒於陛下者也，陛下又何以非群兇而誅之？ 臣往見明敕，自今已後，一依貞觀故事。 且貞觀之時，豈有今日之造寺營觀，加僧尼道士，益無用之官，行不急之務，而亂政者也！ 臣以為棄其言而不行其信，慕其善而不遷其惡，陛下又何以刑於四海？ 往者，和帝之憐悖逆也，為奸人之所誤，宗晉卿勸為第宅，趙履溫勸為園亭，損數百家之居，侵數百家之地。 工徒斫而未息，義兵紛以交馳，卒使亭不得遊，宅不得坐。 信邪佞之說，成骨肉之刑，此陛下之所眼見也。 今茲造觀，臣必知非陛下、公主之本意，得無趙履溫之徒將勸為之，冀誤其骨肉，不可不明察也。 臣聞出家修道者，不預人事，專清其身心，以虛泊為高，以無為為妙，依兩卷《老子》，視一軀天尊，無欲無營，不損不害。 何必璇臺玉榭，寶像珍龕，使人困窮，然後為道哉！ 且舊觀足可歸依，無造無營，以取窮竭。 若此行之三年，國不富，人不安，朝廷不清，陛下不樂，則臣請殺身於朝，以令天下言事者。 伏惟陛下行非常之惠，權停兩觀，以俟豐年。 以兩觀之財，為公主施貧窮，填府庫，則公主福德無窮矣。 不然，臣恐下人怨望，不減於前朝之時。 前朝之時，賢愚知敗，人雖有口而不敢言，言未發聲，禍將及矣。 韋月將受誅於丹僥，燕欽融見殺於紫庭，此人皆不惜其身而納忠於主，身既死矣，朝亦危矣。 故先朝誅之，陛下賞之，是陛下知直言之士有裨於國。 臣今直言，亦先代之直，惟陛下察之。
When Emperor Ruizong acceded, construction again expanded on the two monasteries for the Golden Immortal and Jade Perfected princesses. Earlier, under Emperor Zhongzong, all who had received office through irregular sealed appointments had been dismissed—several hundred or more—and an edict then allowed them to return. Xin Tifou was then Left Remonstrator and again memorialized on current policy, saying: I have often thought that in ancient times, untimely expenditure and improper ranks and rewards brought ruin to families and states—hearing is not as good as seeing. I ask to speak of the successes and failures in governing since Tang began, which Your Majesty has seen with your own eyes. If Your Majesty examines and listens, choosing the good and following it, the enterprise of ten thousand years can naturally be achieved. Why worry that the people will not prosper or that fortune will not endure! Emperor Taizong, the Civil and Martial Sage Emperor, Your Majesty's grandfather, quelled disorder and restored order, established foundations and set the supreme standard, grasped the essence of perfect governance, and instituted simple and essential methods. He reduced officials, purified the bureaucracy, ensured not a single post in the empire was granted idly, and not a single coin of the realm's wealth was wasted. Rewards awaited merit; offices went only to the worthy. Nothing he undertook failed; no one he campaigned against failed to submit. He did not build many temples and monasteries, yet blessings came of themselves; he did not ordain many monks and nuns, yet calamities vanished of themselves. His Way harmonized with Heaven and Earth; his virtue reached the divine spirits. Therefore Heaven and Earth cherished him and the divine spirits protected him, so yin and yang were without fault and wind and rain were timely. The four classes delighted in their occupations; the five grains reached full harvest; surplus grain and silk rotted, filling streets and alleys. From a thousand li, from ten thousand li, tribute flowed to the capital suburbs; The nine Yi and hundred Man tribes submitted allegiance at the palace gates. Since emperors and kings began, none has been so divine and sagely; thus he enjoyed a long reign over many years. Why does Your Majesty not take him as a model? Emperor Zhongzong, the Filial and Harmonious Emperor, Your Majesty's elder brother, inherited his ancestors' enterprise but neglected their transformative teachings; he did not heed worthy counsel but indulged his children's whims. Official ranks were not chosen with care; several thousand idly consumed salaries; Fiefs were granted without merit; over a hundred households improperly held land. He ceaselessly built temples, wasting wealth amounting to tens of billions; He endlessly ordained people, exempting hundreds of thousands from taxes and corvee. This caused state expenditures to increase severalfold while income decreased severalfold. The granaries held no store for a year's end; the treasuries held no silk for a season. Those he disliked were banished, and many of the banished were loyal and good; Those he loved were rewarded, and many of the rewarded were slanderers and villains. Cliques of flatterers chattered incessantly, vying to topple one another. Maintaining one's position at court came not through personal integrity but through factional attachment. He seized the people's food to nourish the cruel and vicious; He stripped clothing from ten thousand to adorn buildings of wood and earth. Consequently men resented and spirits raged, kin were angered and the multitude alienated; floods and droughts were unseasonable and epidemics arose repeatedly. Near and far opinions differed; public and private resources were exhausted. Within five or six years calamities recurred; he did not enjoy a long reign and met his end at the hands of a vicious woman. Temples could not protect his person; monks and nuns could not protect his wife and children. He earned ridicule for ten thousand generations and laughter from the four quarters. This Your Majesty has seen with your own eyes. Why not eradicate and reform it? If Taizong's way of governing is followed, the hundred officials will be well-ordered and the people will have no worries; thus the security of Mount Tai can readily be achieved; If Zhongzong's way of governing is followed, ten thousand people will harbor resentment and a hundred affairs will be unsettled; thus the peril of piled eggs can readily be achieved. Recently since summer continuous rain has not ceased; grain lies wasted in the fields and wheat rots on the threshing grounds. Since autumn began severe drought has brought disaster; seedlings fail to bear fruit, frost and insects ravage, and grass and leaves wither yellow. The common people lament, yet relief is unknown; Yet temple and monastery construction continues daily without pause, and inspector and probationary offices overflow the ministries and bureaus. Your Majesty, loving your two daughters, is building two monasteries for them, burning tiles, transporting timber, carrying earth to fill pits. Street rumors all say the planned cost exceeds a million strings of cash. Your Majesty is a sage; there is nothing you do not know; Your Majesty is an enlightened ruler; there is nothing you do not see. Since you know and see, do you know how many years' stores the granaries hold? How many years' silk the treasuries hold? Do you know whether the common people can survive? Whether supplies can be transported to the three frontiers? At present when a single soldier is dispatched to defend the frontiers or guard the altars of state, most lack clothing and food and all bear hunger and cold. When it comes to rewards and gifts there is nothing to give; armies are suddenly defeated, all for this reason. And yet a million strings of cash are spent to build useless monasteries, incurring the resentment of all within the four seas! Thereby opposing the hearts of ten thousand people! Your Majesty continues the ugly traces of Lady Wei yet does not reform Lady Wei's chaotic governance. You can bear to discard Taizong's fundamental principles of order but cannot bear to discard Zhongzong's steps to chaos; You can bear to discard Taizong's long-term plans but cannot bear to discard Zhongzong's short-sighted schemes. How then will Your Majesty succeed the ancestors and be observed by the myriad states? In the past when Your Majesty was Crown Prince, in Lady Wei's time, you feared peril and ruin and constantly gnashed your teeth at the crowd of villains. Now honored as Son of Heaven, possessing wealth within the seas, if you do not reform the affairs of that crowd of villains, I fear there will again be those who gnash their teeth at Your Majesty. How then can Your Majesty condemn those villains and execute them? I previously saw a clear edict stating that henceforth everything should follow Zhenguan precedents. Moreover in the Zhenguan era was there such building of temples and monasteries, such increase of monks, nuns, and Daoist priests, such multiplication of useless officials, and such pursuit of non-urgent tasks leading to chaotic governance! I believe that to discard their words and not keep faith, to admire their goodness and not change their evils—how then will Your Majesty set an example for all within the four seas? In the past Emperor He's pity for the rebellious was misled by treacherous men. Zong Jinqing urged building mansions; Zhao Luwen urged building gardens and pavilions, destroying the dwellings of several hundred families and encroaching on the land of several hundred families. Craftsmen and laborers hewed without rest; righteous troops rushed about in confusion, until the pavilions could not be enjoyed and the mansions could not be occupied. Believing evil flatterers, he brought punishment upon his own flesh and blood. This Your Majesty has seen with your own eyes. Now in building these monasteries, I know it is not the original intention of Your Majesty and the princesses. Might men like Zhao Luwen be urging it, hoping to mislead your flesh and blood? This must be clearly examined. I have heard that those who leave home to cultivate the Way do not involve themselves in human affairs but purify body and mind, taking emptiness and detachment as lofty and non-action as wondrous, relying on the two scrolls of the Laozi, contemplating the Heavenly Venerable, without desire or striving, without harm or injury. Why must there be jade terraces and jeweled pavilions, precious images and rare shrines, reducing people to poverty and distress, and only then call it the Way! Moreover the old monasteries are sufficient for devotion; do not build, do not strive, thereby causing exhaustion. If after this course is followed for three years the state is not wealthy, the people are not secure, the court is not pure, and Your Majesty is not happy, then I beg to be executed at court as a warning to all who speak on affairs under Heaven. I humbly beg Your Majesty to exercise extraordinary grace, temporarily halting the two monasteries until a year of plenty. Use the wealth for the two monasteries to allow the princesses to give alms to the poor and fill the treasuries; then the princesses' blessings and virtue will be boundless. If not, I fear popular resentment will be no less than in the previous reign. In the previous reign the worthy and foolish knew ruin was coming; though men had mouths they dared not speak. Before words were uttered calamity was about to strike. Wei Yuejiang was executed at Dandiao; Yan Qinrong was killed in the Purple Court. These men did not cherish their own lives but offered loyalty to their lord. With their lives gone, the court was also endangered. Therefore the previous reign executed them but Your Majesty rewards them. This shows Your Majesty knows that outspoken scholars benefit the state. My outspoken words now are also the outspokenness of former generations. I beg Your Majesty to consider this.
20
疏奏，睿宗嘉其公直。 稍遷為右臺殿中侍御史。 開元中，累轉潁王府長史。 天寶初卒，年八十余。 史臣曰：夫好聞其善，惡聞其過，君人者之常情也； 寧諂媚以取容，不逆耳以招禍，臣人者之常情也。 能反此者，不亦善乎！ 李、薛等六君，吐忠讜之言，補朝廷之失，有犯無隱，不愧古人，有唐之良臣也。 贊贊曰：臣之事君，有邪有正。 君之使臣，從諫則聖。 李、薛輸忠，救人之命。 韋、韓讜言，醫國之病。 辛、王章疏，犯顏竦聽。 張子法言，實裨時政。
Emperor Ruizong praised his fairness and uprightness when the memorial was submitted. He was soon made Palace Censor of the Right Bureau. In Kaiyuan he rose to chief administrator of the Prince of Ying's household. He died early in Tianbao at over eighty. The historiographer writes: To love hearing praise and hate hearing fault is the common disposition of rulers; to prefer flattery for favor rather than unwelcome words that invite disaster is the common disposition of ministers. To reverse this—is that not excellence itself? Li, Xue, and the other six spoke loyal and forthright words, repaired the court's failings, and offended without concealment. They did not disgrace the ancients—they were worthy ministers of Tang. Commentary: In how ministers serve their ruler, there is the crooked and the straight. In how rulers employ ministers, to heed remonstrance is sagely. Li and Xue offered loyalty and saved lives. Wei and Han spoke bluntly and cured the state's ills. Xin and Wang submitted forthright memorials that made the ruler listen in awe. Zhang's words accorded with law and truly benefited governance.
